newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mass demonstrations planned over Zimbabwe strike.
newsitem.headline: Mass demonstrations planned over Zimbabwe strike.

text.p: Zimbabwean trade unions, churches and human rights groups called for mass demonstrations on Monday to press President Robert Mugabe's embattled government to resolve a costly strike by doctors and nurses.
But the government vowed on Friday it would maintain a tough stance against the strikers, saying they were guilty of crippling the southern African country's public health system.

Spokesmen for the Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU), the Zimbabwe Human Rights Organisation (Zimrights), the Public Service Association (PSA) union and the Zimbabwe Council of Churches (ZCC) said their organisations agreed on Thursday to organise demonstrations over the strike.

"We as ZCTU are deeply concerned about the impact on the health sector and therefore call upon any concerned to join us in expressing our national outrage over the lack of sensitivity on the part of government on this matter," ZCTU secretary-general Morgan Tsvangirayi told reporters.

"We are mobilising for this demonstration, but what will follow if government does not listen and bring normalcy to the health sector, remains to be seen," he said of the strike which has forced the closure of the country's two largest hospitals, and which angry relatives say has led to many unnecessary deaths.
"Government insensitity cannot be tolerated anymore," Tsvangirayi said.

Acting Public Service, Labour and Social Welfare Minister Nathan Shamuyarira stoutly defended the government, saying it was willing to discuss the strikers' grievances over pay and working conditions but would not submit to blackmail.
He said the government would not reverse its decision to fire all strikers, saying it was advertising for nurses and doctors in Britain, South Africa and other African states to replace those sacked.

An estimated 10,000 nurses have been on strike since October 21, and they were joined this week by about 300 doctors who were angry at the arrest of two union colleagues accused of inciting the strike.

Doctors Farai Jiah and Austin Bene -- both leaders of the state Hospitals Doctors Association -- were freed on Wednesday by a Harare court which said it needed time to decide whether to refer their case to the Supreme Court as their lawyer had raised constitutional issues during an initial remand hearing.

But the doctors, and other medical staff mainly at Zimbabwe's two largest hospitals, have stayed on the streets with the nurses, saying they will only resume work when the government addresses their pay demands and reinstates those fired.

"We are standing firm on our principles that doctors and nurses should not use the strike as a weapon. That door is closed and it is not going to be useful because they will get nothing in the area of the strike," minister Shamuyarira said.
Municipal clinics and private surgeries have come under heavy pressure after the closure of Harare and Parirenyatwa hospitals.
